title: EU Commits €10 Billion to Build Seven AI Gigafactories in Global Compute Race
excerpt: The European Commission expanded its AI infrastructure plan from five to seven gigafactories after strong demand from member states, with AMD, Nvidia, and Qualcomm signing on as chip suppliers.
body:
• The EU will invest €10 billion ($11.5 billion) in seven AI gigafactories combining advanced processors, cloud technology, and data centers
  • The plan expanded from five to seven sites after strong interest from EU countries, with the aim of attracting €20 billion in private investment
  • AMD, Nvidia, and Qualcomm have signed letters of intent to supply chips for the project
  • Tender closes November 12, with winners announced early 2027 and facilities operational within 18 months of contract signing

Europe's Biggest AI Bet

The European Commission announced Thursday it will fund seven artificial intelligence gigafactories across the bloc with €10 billion ($11.5 billion), its most aggressive move yet to close the computing gap with the United States and China, according to Reuters.

Each facility will combine advanced AI processors, software platforms, cloud technology, high-speed connectivity, and data centers into integrated computing hubs. The plan, originally designed for five sites, was expanded to seven after EU member states showed stronger-than-expected interest in hosting the infrastructure.

"Access to the raw scale of computing power within AI Gigafactories is a strategic necessity for Europe as AI development accelerates."

— Henna Virkkunen, EU tech chief

The Commission aims to attract at least €20 billion in additional private investment. Consortia, special-purpose vehicles, technology providers, cloud service companies, and public entities can all apply to participate.

Chip Giants Sign On

Three of the world's largest semiconductor companies — AMD, Nvidia, and Qualcomm — have signed letters of intent with the Commission to provide chips to groups involved in the gigafactory projects, Reuters reported. Their participation signals that the EU's initiative has secured buy-in from the industry's biggest players.

The tender process will close on November 12, 2026. The Commission expects to announce successful bidders in early 2027, with the facilities becoming operational within 18 months of contract signing.

The seven gigafactories will supplement the 19 existing AI factories already operating across EU countries. Earlier phases of the program deployed five AI-optimized supercomputers in Finland, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, and Sweden, with Spain's MareNostrum 5 upgraded and a new facility planned in Greece, according to Data Center Dynamics.

Scale of the Challenge

The gigafactories represent a different order of magnitude from existing infrastructure. According to analysis by Notebookcheck citing UBS modeling, each facility is expected to cost €3-5 billion, house at least 100,000 high-end GPUs, and deliver several times the compute capacity of Europe's largest existing AI clusters.

A full buildout of 10-15 such plants would add roughly 1.5 to 2 gigawatts of IT load — about 15 percent of Europe's current data center capacity. Power delivery is expected to be the binding constraint. A single gigafactory could draw a full gigawatt, comparable to a midsize nuclear power plant.

The initiative sits alongside the broader InvestAI fund, a €20 billion public-private partnership announced earlier in 2026, designed to give European startups and SMEs access to large-scale AI training and inference infrastructure.

Global Context

The EU's push comes as the United States and China continue to pour resources into AI infrastructure. Brussels argues it has roughly 30 percent more AI researchers per capita than the United States but lacks the computing power to match their output.

For Indian tech professionals working across European markets, the gigafactory buildout could create significant opportunities in AI engineering, data center operations, and cloud infrastructure. India's growing IT services sector already provides substantial talent to European technology projects, and the scale of the EU's ambition will likely increase demand for skilled AI practitioners in the region.
